description: Hello everyone! I am  Rayyan Muhammad (Shinwari), an enthusiastic computer science undergraduate with a strong academic foundation and practical project experience. My technical interests and core competencies include software engineering principles, data structures, relational database management (SQL/MariaDB), and machine learning pipelines developed using Python (Pandas and Scikit-Learn).
summary: A fullstack web app that turns NASA HLS Sentinel-2 satellite change data into ambient music and cell-by-cell NDVI sonification — so you can hear how any place on Earth has changed between two years, not just see it on a map.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Earth Jukebox is a fullstack web application that converts NASA satellite change data into sound. A user searches any location on Earth (or picks from curated study areas like Kaghan Valley, Swat, Hunza, or Islamabad), selects two years to compare, and sets a study-area radius. The app then runs a NASA HLS Sentinel-2 temporal change analysis, produces a real 3-band GeoTIFF (NDVI, NDMI, and NBR change indices), decodes it in the browser, and generates two audio outputs: a 53-second ambient composition driven by five environmental layers (vegetation, water, snow, burned area, temperature), and a cell-by-cell NDVI sonification that plays one tone per grid cell in row-major order, with pitch rising for vegetation gain and dropping for loss.

The pipeline has five stages. First, location search geocodes a place name via Nominatim. Second, the backend queries the NASA/HLS/HLSS30/v002 collection, filters to the June–October growing season, discovers the MGRS tiles intersecting the area, downloads each scene, masks cloud-contaminated pixels using Fmask bits, and computes per-year median composites. Third, the frontend decodes the resulting GeoTIFF with geotiff.js, extracting transform, bounds, CRS, and three change bands. Fourth, the music engine reads the four-band environmental raster, downsamples it to a 16×16 grid, normalizes values, and flattens them into a 64-beat sequence synthesized as PCM 16-bit audio. Fifth, the NDVI sonification endpoint turns every grid cell into a 0.12-second tone with a follow-along highlight synced to the audio.

What benefits does it have?

The primary benefit is making NASA Earth science legible to non-technical audiences. Spectral indices like NDVI, NDMI, and NBR are powerful measurements, but they are inherently visual and numerical — green-and-red maps that most people cannot interpret. By translating those same measurements into sound, Earth Jukebox gives them an emotional dimension. A listener can hear the magnitude and pace of change in a way a color ramp cannot convey. It also produces real, downloadable artifacts: a valid GeoTIFF that can be loaded into any GIS tool, and a WAV file that can be shared, embedded, or played in any media player.

The app is accessible by design. Screen-reader live regions announce the backend status, processing stage, and each NDVI cell value as it plays. Every interactive element is keyboard navigable. The layout is mobile-first with 44-pixel touch targets, and the color palette meets WCAG AA contrast on every surface. This is not an add-on; accessibility was a first-class requirement from the start.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to open a new modality for environmental communication. Decision-makers, educators, journalists, and citizens who would never open QGIS or read a remote-sensing paper can listen to how their valley, their forest, or their watershed has changed. It creates an emotional connection to data that maps alone cannot establish. For educators, it is a tool for teaching spectral indices and change detection without requiring students to learn GIS. For communicators, it is a way to make climate and land-change stories memorable. For the NASA Earth Information Center mission, it demonstrates that open satellite data can reach entirely new audiences when paired with creative translation layers.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

The frontend is built with Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, and TypeScript 5, styled with Tailwind CSS 4 and the shadcn/ui component library. The interactive map uses react-leaflet v5, and GeoTIFF decoding in the browser uses geotiff.js. Client state is managed with Zustand and server state with TanStack Query. Animations use Framer Motion.

The backend is Python 3.12 with FastAPI, served by uvicorn. NumPy handles array math, SciPy writes the WAV files, and rasterio reads and writes GeoTIFF rasters. Place-name geocoding uses geopy with the Nominatim service. The Earth Engine Python API is optionally integrated for live NASA HLS access. Pydantic v2 validates every request. The backend runs as a double-fork daemon alongside the Next.js dev server, with an instrumentation hook that auto-spawns it.

The data source is NASA/HLS/HLSS30/v002, the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 product, at 30-meter resolution. The app also ships curated NASA Scientific Visualization Studio presets for the EIC Visualization Studio. No special hardware is required — it runs on any modern browser.

How is your project creative?

Earth Jukebox is creative in three ways. First, it is the first system to sonify HLS change rasters cell-by-cell with a follow-along highlight synced to the backend's exact timing (0.12-second tone, 0.02-second gap, 0.25-second row pause). Second, it uses zero mock data — every single tone is synthesized from a real raster pixel value, so the audio is a faithful, not decorative, representation of the data. Third, it pairs two output modalities: a composed ambient track where each environmental layer is a musical voice, and a raw sonification where every cell is heard individually. This dual approach lets users choose between an artistic overview and a precise, cell-level reading.

The EIC Visualization Studio adds another creative layer: users can bring a NASA visualization asset and explicitly confirm that an existing HLS dataset matches its variable, geography, and time period before enabling sonification. The app never infers the underlying dataset — it requires user-confirmed pairing, which is an honest approach to data integrity.

What factors did your team consider?

The team considered data integrity first. The app never fabricates a connection between an EIC visualization and a dataset; the user must explicitly confirm the match. When Earth Engine is unavailable, the app honestly reports HLS as using a synthetic fallback rather than pretending to serve live satellite data.

Accessibility was considered from the first component, not bolted on. Screen-reader support, keyboard navigation, and contrast standards shaped every design decision. Performance mattered: the HLS per-scene download workflow avoids creating one oversized Earth Engine request, instead downloading each scene as a compact GeoTIFF and computing composites locally. Architectural honesty mattered: the proxy layer means the browser never sees the backend port, and the backend can be swapped at runtime. And scientific accuracy mattered: the music engine mirrors the Python functions.py layer-by-layer and band-by-band, so the TypeScript and Python backends produce structurally identical output.
dataRefs: NASA HLS S30 v002 (Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2)
